messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 60
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Hotel Manager
  trauma_type: Toxic chemical exposure
  pcl5: 68

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Body Monitoring: constantly check body for signs of danger or injury, Avoid Reminders: Being reminded of the event by others, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns, Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to, Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
  Negative Appraisals: Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Sokha is a 60-year-old Cambodian American man who has worked for years as a hotel manager, a role he once valued because he knew how to keep a busy building calm and orderly. The event that still organizes his life began during a maintenance emergency at the hotel, when a cleaning chemical was accidentally mixed in a poorly ventilated service area. He remembers the sharp, acrid taste that hit the back of his throat almost immediately, the metallic-bleach flavor that made him gag and convinced him something was entering his body that he could not stop. In the confusion, staff were coughing, a guest was shouting, and Sokha could not tell who had been exposed or how serious it was. What stayed with him most was the sensation that his own body had betrayed him in the very moment he needed it; he has come away certain that he cannot trust his body to warn him properly or protect him, and with a broader feeling that bad things can happen to him without any way to prevent them.

In the weeks after, those beliefs hardened rather than fading. If he felt a dryness in his throat, a change in his breathing, or a strange taste while drinking coffee, he took it as proof that his body was unreliable and that danger could already be underway before he understood it. Because he had come to believe he could not stop bad things from happening, he began checking himself repeatedly for signs of injury or exposure, pressing at his throat, noticing his breathing, scanning for any sensation that might mean the chemicals had done lasting damage. The same beliefs spread outward into how he moved through the hotel. He watched hallways, housekeeping carts, maintenance closets, and the expressions on staff faces for signs that something was wrong. He also pulled away from reminders, cutting off conversations when employees mentioned the spill or later safety changes, because being reminded of it felt less like remembering and more like being returned to a moment in which he was helpless again.

The memories themselves have remained unusually immediate. He does not simply think about the exposure; at unpredictable moments the memory forces itself into his mind, and when it does he can taste that same chemical bitterness as if it is on his tongue again. Standing near the laundry room at work, catching the smell of industrial cleaners, or hearing a guest complain that a room smells “too strong” can make him feel, for a few seconds, as though the event is happening right now. Those moments have reinforced his conviction that his body cannot be trusted and that he is not really at home anywhere anymore. He says the hotel used to feel like his place, but now every back corridor and supply room can turn unfamiliar in an instant, and even at home he feels set apart, as if he no longer belongs in ordinary life with people who are not braced for something toxic to happen.

Because the memories arrive so forcefully, he has become more vigilant and more avoidant over time. When an intrusive image or the chemical taste comes back during a shift, he starts checking the air vents, looking for leaks, watching staff movements, and monitoring his chest and throat. He may reroute himself away from the service areas for the rest of the day or abruptly end a discussion if someone starts revisiting the incident. These habits give him brief relief, but they also keep his attention fixed on signs of threat. The more he scans his body and surroundings, the more easily normal sensations or small delays become loaded with danger; if housekeeping is late answering a radio call, he is quick to assume something bad has happened. Once that fear spikes, his body goes tense and ready, and in that state the memory becomes even easier to trigger. A routine pause outside a chemical storage room can bring back the taste, the panic, and the sense of being trapped in the original exposure.

Over months, this has tightened into a daily pattern. His body feels constantly on alert, and false alarms are frequent; a harmless smell, a cough from a staff member, or a late response over the hotel radio can make him react as if there is an immediate emergency. That alarm then confirms, in his mind, that he was right not to trust his body or the world around him. He becomes more certain that he cannot prevent bad things, more convinced that he does not belong in spaces other people move through casually, and more dependent on checking, scanning, and shutting down reminders. At work this has changed how he manages. Staff have noticed that he hovers near maintenance issues, repeatedly asks whether anyone feels dizzy or unwell, and avoids longer debriefs about safety procedures if they come too close to the day of the spill. At home, his partner sees him go quiet after certain smells or after delays that other people would dismiss, and then watch his own breathing for long stretches.

By the time he sought help, Sokha was exhausted by how quickly an ordinary workday could become a scene of danger in his mind and body. What finally pushed him into treatment was realizing that a minor cleaning complaint from a guest had left him shaking, tasting the chemicals again, and unable to finish the conversation without stepping out to check himself in the mirror. He is frightened that this will keep shrinking his life and his work until there is nowhere he feels safe or at ease. At the same time, he is hoping that treatment might help him trust his body enough to stop living as if another exposure is always about to happen.
